prompt.context: Our client is a start-up with the ability to deliver broadband internet to commercial airlines. There are 3,000 commercial planes in the market. The start-up would have to invest relatively little and would keep most revenues. Airlines would charge customers on a per-flight pricing model.
prompt.question: How would you help the client think about their offering? Begin by estimating the market size for broadband for airlines, then evaluate the feasibility of entering this market.

clarifying_info.a: The company holds the patent on the high-speed connection technology, giving it a defensible IP position.

clarifying_info.q: What revenue level is needed to be profitable?
clarifying_info.a: If the company can generate $250,000 per plane in annual revenue, it will be profitable.

clarifying_info.q: Is there existing demand from airlines?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, there is general interest from airlines in offering broadband to passengers.

exhibits.title: Flight and Passenger Data
exhibits.shows: Data on the number of flights, legs per plane per year, and passenger mix by type (business vs. leisure) to support market sizing
exhibits.data: Relevant figures on annual flight legs per plane and passenger counts — use to estimate total addressable market

exhibits.title: Price Sensitivity / Penetration Curve
exhibits.shows: A table or chart showing the relationship between broadband price per flight and the percentage of laptop-carrying passengers who would purchase
exhibits.data: At $5 price point higher penetration; at $15 approximately 20% penetration among laptop users; at $25 lower penetration — exact figures shown in exhibit

framework: Market Size — estimate total revenue opportunity: number of planes, flights per plane per year, passengers per flight, laptop penetration, price sensitivity/elasticity, and segmentation (business vs. leisure)
Go to Market — pricing and revenue model (per-flight charge), launch strategy, installation capabilities, maintenance and training
Risks — barriers to entry, FAA and regulatory considerations, existing and emerging competition, capital investment required, airline and broader economic risk

questions.prompt: Estimate the total annual market size for in-flight broadband across the 3,000-plane fleet.
questions.guidance: Candidate should build up from number of planes → legs per plane per year → passengers per leg → laptop-carrying passengers → likely purchasers at a given price. Should acknowledge segmentation (business travelers more likely to pay) and price elasticity. A strong candidate references Exhibit 1 for flight/passenger data and Exhibit 2 for penetration rates.

math.setup: Use Exhibit 1 data for legs/plane/year and passenger counts; use Exhibit 2 penetration rates at chosen price point. Illustrative path: 3,000 planes × annual legs per plane × passengers per leg × laptop penetration × purchase rate × price.
steps: Identify legs per plane per year from Exhibit 1 (approximately 2,000 legs/plane/year)
Assume ~100 passengers per leg with ~50 laptop users per leg
At $15 price point, Exhibit 2 shows ~20% penetration → 10 users/leg
math.answer: ~$900M total annual market; approximately $300,000 per plane per year

questions.prompt: Perform a breakeven analysis: what price and penetration rate allows the client to reach profitability?
questions.guidance: Candidate should connect the $250,000/plane profitability threshold to legs per plane and required users per leg. Should test multiple price/penetration combinations from Exhibit 2 and identify the optimal price. Strong candidates compare combinations systematically and pick $15 as the revenue-maximizing price point.

math.setup: Profitability threshold = $250,000/plane/year. With 2,000 legs/plane/year, required revenue per leg = $250,000 / 2,000 = $125/leg.
steps: At $15/user → need $125 / $15 ≈ 8.3 users/leg to break even
Exhibit 2: at $15, ~20% of 50 laptop users = 10 users/leg → exceeds breakeven
Check other price points (assuming 100 passengers per flight):
$15 yields the highest revenue per leg at $300, well above $125 breakeven
math.answer: Set price at $15/flight; this yields ~$300/leg and ~$600,000/plane/year, exceeding the $250,000 profitability threshold. Breakeven requires only ~8 users/leg at $15.

questions.prompt: What other factors should the client consider before entering this market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should demonstrate breadth on market entry factors beyond market size and breakeven. Key areas: competitive dynamics (IP/patent protection), regulatory risk (FAA approval for in-flight connectivity hardware), go-to-market and installation logistics, capital requirements, airline partnership risk, and economic sensitivity of air travel demand.

brainstorming.prompt: What risks and other factors should the client consider when evaluating this market entry?

categories.name: Competitive & IP
ideas: Client holds the patent — strong moat, but duration and enforceability matter
Watch for emerging competitors developing alternative technologies
Evaluate whether patent covers all relevant geographies

categories.name: Regulatory & FAA
ideas: FAA must approve any hardware installed on commercial aircraft
Certification timelines can be lengthy and costly
International routes require compliance with multiple aviation authorities

categories.name: Go-to-Market & Operations
ideas: Need airline partnerships or direct contracts for installation
Installation logistics across 3,000 planes requires scale and coordination
Ongoing maintenance and support capabilities must be built or outsourced
Training for airline staff on the system

categories.name: Financial & Capital
ideas: Capital investment for hardware per plane even if modest
Revenue share arrangement with airlines needs to be negotiated
Pricing model (per-flight vs. subscription vs. tiered) affects uptake

categories.name: Market & Economic Risk
ideas: Airline industry is cyclical; demand drops sharply in recessions
Business travel (higher WTP) is more sensitive to corporate budget cuts
Leisure travelers have lower willingness to pay for in-flight WiFi

recommendation: The client should enter the market. At the recommended price of $15 per flight, the model generates approximately $300,000 per plane annually — exceeding the $250,000 profitability threshold — against a total addressable market of ~$900M across 3,000 planes.
The proprietary patent provides a meaningful competitive barrier, and the relatively low required investment makes the risk/reward attractive.
risks: FAA regulatory approval process may delay launch and add unforeseen costs
Patent could be challenged or designed around by competitors
Airline industry cyclicality could reduce passenger volumes and willingness to pay
Dependence on airline partners for installation and distribution creates execution risk
next_steps: Initiate FAA certification process for the hardware
Negotiate pilot agreements with 1-2 airline partners to validate installation, pricing, and demand
Conduct deeper customer research on price sensitivity across business vs. leisure segments
Model out capital requirements and phased rollout plan across the 3,000-plane fleet
